I really enjoyed this game.

While being mainly text-based with you, the player, handling a software interface it still managed to adhere well to the 'rollercoaster' feeling of calm and thrill. The story is well-told and the choices feel like they matter in the way they smartly weave back into the ongoing plot and changes the outcomes of various actions.

The music is pleasantly laid-back with appropriate stings when the situation calls for it, and the overall art is very endearing.

Only thing I missed during my two replays was either a means of using save slots myself so I could decide a point I wanted to start from (rather than replaying an entire chapter), or an added skip button for conversations I've already seen in my first playthrough. Some of the conversations are very long and do not change their content, and I grew impatient waiting for them to scroll through a second and third time while trying to get back to where I wanted to be to explore different options.

A story game where you play as a curator of information to try and help the actual authorities solve a case. Pretty interesting story revelations/twists.

Information you submit determines how the story plays out (so instead of feeding all information and looking at the big picture you're selecting information to make the people act the way you want).

However, there are some unrealisms/restrictions/forced guessing to make the story flow faster. In one example, you're not allowed to determine the destination of a bank transfer and are forced to guess and submit.

Instead of submitting facts as individual data points and looking at the big picture, it extrapolates and takes things as broad facts in a wider scope. You can't submit any context (heated argument, hearsay, depiction of others from one perspective).

Anything you submit to Orwell is taken as fact and representative of the person (instead of one data point in their life). Sometimes the conclusions drawn from the information don't really match what you submit (so be sure to look at the tooltip) and are a bit of a stretch and (sometimes intentionally!) out of context.

Worth a look if you like the idea/concept of being the gatekeeper of information in an investigation.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] Gold/yellow data chunks are important ones ('conflicts') that have a big part in determining what happens.
[*] Reactions to events/information are sometimes extreme.
[*] It would be nice to be able to see (or construct) a visual timeline of events. It can get confusing (if only using memory) when thinking about what happened on which day and what events occurred before/after another event.
[*] I didn't like part of the ending. The argument is that [spoiler]they are forced to prosecute based on what you put into Orwell. But it's not like humans are automated; once the human element is introduced in the process they can ignore/deny/hide the order to prosecute and not actually carry it out. And orders to prosecute (I would think) aren't automatically shown to the public.[/spoiler]
[/list]

[h1] ORWELL REVIEW [/h1]


[b] What is Orwell? [/b] 
Orwell is a story-driven puzzle/mystery game in which you, someone outside 'The Nation', take control of Orwell - the latest security system designed to counteract terrorism, etc. Its a game that focuses more on giving you an experience with its story and plot rather than with engaging gameplay. 

[u] STORY [/u] 
Orwell isn't shy in showing its influences from George Orwells '1984' (clearly), and thats a good thing. '1984' is considered by many to be one of the best pieces of literature ever written, and with very good reason - it predicts a horrible shift in society which results in a dystopian state run with an iron fist and constant survelliance and information control on its populace. George Orwell's novel takes place after this dytopian rule has been established for years, so we do not truly understand how it became so all-powerful to begin with, however, Orwell takes a look at what it may be like at the start of this rule, with a brand new system, called ORWELL, being used to solve a terror attack on 'The Nation'. When Orwell wrote '1984' there was no internet, or social media, etc. and this game takes a look at how '1984' would be had those things been considered, and trying to basically update '1984' for a modern audience and make it culturally relevant today is no small feat, and happily, I can say they have done a superb job of capturing, while updating, George Orwell's original vision.  

Overall Story Score = 9/10 (Masterful) 


[u] GAMEPLAY [/u]
Gameplay in Orwell is probably the games weakest point as there's not much actual 'gameplay' involved. For the most part Orwell's gameplay consists of reading text documents, web pages, phonecall logs, emails, etc. and finding relevant text and info and attaching it to certain peoples files. While this may sound completely mundane it is actually quite a refreshing take on detective gameplay and feels like you are genuinely investigating people. Although, personally, towards the climax of the game I found trying to find that one last clue to tie things together quite frustrating and slowed the pace of the game. 

Overall Gameplay Score = 6/10 (Good)


[u] GRAPHICS [/u] 
Orwell uses a rather unique cell-shaded polygon art style, very similar to something you would find in a visual novel, and it compliments the game well. As someone who isnt a huge fan of completely drawn art styles Ifound myself really liking the approach this game took in its art direction. 

Overall Graphics Score = 7/10 (Great) 


[u] SOUND [/u] 
Orwell has a nice relaxing soundtrack for the most part with occasional moments of high intensity. The soundtrack perfectly fits the game and was particularly noticable during certain parts of the game which greatly increased the impact of those moments. Also, the soundtrack doesn't get annoying or repetative at any point which is impressive considering the length of time you are listening to it. Saying all that though, its by no means a memorable soundtrack or anything special. 

Overall Sound Score = 6/10 (Good) 


[u] LASTING APPEAL [/u] 
It took me roughly 4 hours to play through the story once, and I am plannign at some point to play through it once more, but that will probably be the max I play. I personally wouldn't pay full price just purely due to the price-to-playtime ratio but on sale I would definitely pick it up. Overall though the lasting appeal is quite poor due to it being a story driven game all based on a whodunnit payoff, which makes replayability a bit less appealing. There are multiple endings however so if you want to get all of them you may get more out of it than most.

Overall Lasting Appeal Score = 4/10 (Below Average)


[b] OVERALL SCORE = 7/10 - Great [/b]

Orwell fails on a lot of levels. A lot of very fundamental writing levels. First and foremost it gives you a set of tools that allow you to see what people do on the internet and tasks you with finding the perpetrator of a bombing. You're given one prime suspect and as you progress your web of people of interest grows and grows. The principle gameplay mechanic involves choosing which specific pieces of information you choose to report to your orwellian system. Which will change how the game plays out. The first failure comes that it is often very obvious what information is going to affect what, as it is all highlighted in blue, or yellow if it conflicts with another piece of information. This is another problem. The conflict system makes very little sense most of the time. One of the first examples of the system in use involves a personal blog ran by a Person of Interest and an editorial they wrote for a newspaper. They both detail the same concept but with completely differeing opinions on the matter, and these pieces of information are considered a conflict and therefore cannot both be reported. While this specific instance makes very little gameplay difference either way it still makes no sense. Being able to report both pieces of information would have shown (at least to me) his willingness to play whatever side of an issue would get him paid, and could've sowed him as a much stronger suspect later on. Instead you have instances where you handler is confused by information you weren't able to provide them due to it being a conflict, when both pieces of information were true. This creates a very frustrating experience in trying to influence the story and with trying to keep information that is relevant to the story seperate from information that isnt. Another fundamental failing of the story telling is its ending, which if I'm perfectly honest; is godawful. To my knowledge, your choices throughout the game have no impact on the ending. There's just three buttons at the end. Push one for your ending. None of them making  a bit of sense. Right before your ending the perpetrator of the bombings reveals themselves, showing that the previous three chapters had all just been misdirection to make sure no player could possibly guess the real one and they basically say to you the player "And this is why your system doesn't work! You couldn't even figure out I was the perpetrator" When it was the game mechanics and information that was provided to you by the game that made it impossible to determine the perpetrator. They then ask you to take down the system, since you can now see it doesnt work. your other two options are to get a politician associated with your orwell system arrested, or to claim the group the perpetrator belongs to are all terrorists using out of context IMs. If you're thinking that this seems to be lacking a very obvious fourth option then I agree. My first instinct was simply to use the perpetrator admitting to instigating the bombings to get her arrested. As that would make sense, she admitted it to our face and yet there's no option present. Just the three arbitrary ones presented. In the end it was three chapters of intriguing build up for one chapter of letdowns and unguessable twists that completely kill the narrative, suspension of disbelief, and immersion. 4/10

A truly fantastic game of detective work and morality. 

You absolutely need to be in the right frame of mind to enjoy it(should you play it like it was any generic game, you'll likely end up disappointed. You have to appraoch it in a cerebral manner to get most out of it). The gameplay is very interesting as it evolves cleverly through the game. The storytelling is executed flawlessly both in quality and flow. 

Perhaps the most interesting part of the game is the subtleness. While the main plotline is told in full, should you play through it "correctly", there are plenty of minor details that are never referred to, but can be deduced logically. 

I was extremely pleased with myself when I deduced the truth behind what was going on by halfway of Episode 4 through simply thinking about it and going through loads of old data. Then, in Episode 5 I got to reach the conclusions I had made, although in an entirely different manner. The way I had analyzed the truth was very different from how the game presented it ultimately. However, all the pieces of information were in the game, just hidden in a slightly different way. A blog post made a day after one certain event happened, a few innocent referrals to seemingly mundane things that put together paint a very interesting picture, and so on. I use this as an example of how expertly crafted the whole experience is. Every single detail has been crafted with painstaking detail, and there are many 'untold secrets' that imply a great deal under the surface. Personal drama for characters that's never made explicit, motivations of characters only left as implications from their personal data, and so on. I can't give it enough praise.

Not only is the writing extremely clever, it's also amazingly coordinated and detailed. It's a true masterpiece of game-storytelling. I never would've guessed I'd like it as much as I did, but in the end it reached a very exclusive spot in my hierarchy of games with very few peers.

Still, it's certainly not a game for everyone. 

PS The ethics and moral problems presented in the game are treated in a very careful manner. While there's an underlying biasedness in the game(as is obvious in the title), it's executed in an incredibly skilled way. Not once did I think it was hamfisted or "obvious" or such. Everything made sense and nothing was purely black-and-white. It's quite the feat, since the inspiration for the game, 1984, is a hamfisted load of nonsense that made me roll my eyes with every page on how unrealistic and stupid it was. This game, however, is pure genius.

I haven't [i]cared[/i] this deeply about a game in a LONG time. This invested. This engrossed. Possessing such a strong sense that this game [b]matters[/b]. If videogames are studied as an art form at some point in the future, and their impact (or potential thereof) upon culture measured, this game will be seen as prophetic.

The premise is very simple: you are sitting at Big Brother's keyboard. There's a terrorist attack, and it's up to you to find the guilty party and bring them to justice. But all the while, you are made acutely aware that your actions have very real, often very immediate consequences. You are digging into people's lives—innocent as often as guilty, possibly even more so—and with every datachunk you choose to upload to the main server, the government has yet more information they have no business knowing, much less acting upon. The results of your choices WILL haunt you: there's no way down the rabbit hole that isn't painful, and there's no way back up. In later episodes, the system itself and the history behind its creation comes into question, and it's up to you to decide the fate of a nation.

The characters in the game are very intelligently written. Many have secrets you may or may not uncover. Some prove to be [i]very[/i] different from what you may first expect once you research them—or they research you. Expect your emotions to be challenged. The scenarios are surprisingly believable, and astoundingly branchable; the game starts to feel very unscripted by the end, which is quite possibly the best compliment I can give the entire game.

If it weren't horrendously ironic for me to say this, given the nature of the game, I'd say that Orwell is as [i]literally[/i] required playing as any game can get. I can't recommend it enough.

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
Orwell takes place in a distopian near future in the fictional city of Bonton in The Nation. Orwell is the codename of a vastly advanced surveilance system. They outsource investigations to outsiders of the nation - you! It is your task to spy on suspects and inform the government of what is going on. Basically, you roleplay as "Mr. FBI Man".

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Interesting Story[/b] - The game is divided into five chapters, each representing a day in game. I won't be spoiling anything here so there isn't much to say, but I will state my overall impression. The story is good! If you take everything at face value you'll be in for a surprise when you realise this game is not as shallow as it may seem. Each chapter unveils another layer of mystery. There are also three endings (more on that later).

[*][b]Some Replayability[/b] - Every chapter has a few endings (usually two or three). After you finish the game, you may choose to replay starting from any chapter (subsequent ones are erased). Most unique paths you can take are linked to an achievement, so 100%-ing the game is pretty much just exploring every possibility. Don't get too exited though, as that took me about 8 hours and two playthroughs (but in the second one I did consult a guide to save time).

[*][b]Clean UI[/b] - I really like the clean, very intuitive interface. Which is good, considering as this UI is basically the whole game itself. The only downside is that it does not have a dark mode for playing at night, but it's not a dealbreaker.
[/list]

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Hand Holding[/b] - You give information to Orwell by drag and dropping data chunks from your spy browser to the Orwell app. They are automatically outlined for you, which seems stupid, but it's a necesarry evil if you think about the programmers. However, one thing I don't like are the special chunks - the conflicts are highlighted in yellow, even if you didn't find both. This makes you extra careful before uploading as one makes the other invalid. This is how the story branches, but if you think about it it's a little stupid. How does the browser know about the conflict if you didn't access the other data chunk yet? This should be up to you - the "detective" to figure out. I wish they were all blue all the time, or turn yellow only after discovering both.

[*][b]Choices Almost Don't Matter[/b] - Remember when I said chapters? Well... they're pretty much isolated instances. Outcomes are mentioned from one to another, but only through slight dialogue changes. But the story progresses the same no matter what you do, until you reach chapter five and finally get to choose an ending.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Orwell is a good game because it explores an interesting concept and offers a good story to boot. While it's not as mindbending as I first expected, I still recommended it as a very interactive visual novel. If the topic interests you and don't mind the short playtime, this is a good game to pick up.

[h1] Orwell Review[/h1]

The story of Orwell takes place in a fictional country where its citizens are being spied on by a government that basically has access to everything. You play an investigator who starts his or her job right as a terrorist bomb goes off, and it becomes your job to solve the mystery of who is to blame.

What Orwell does well really good, is in building up the mystery. As an investigator, you have access to the game's Namesake Orwell which seems to be a computer, or program that like an octopus has its tentacles in everything. This allows you to listen in on phone calls and read emails, all for the purpose of figuring out who is the bad guy.

But what Orwell does even better is blur the line between what is a good guy and what is a bad guy, and the adventure albeit behind the keyboard, leads you to a realization that maybe things are not as they seem.

What I really enjoyed about the game was its art style, and the way the game is able to take something meant to be very flat and paint a beautiful world as you discover more and more evidence.

It's Pros:

[list]
    [*] + The game is beautiful.
    [*] + The mystery is genuine, by that I mean nothing is easy to figure out.
    [*] + The music is enchanting
[/list]

It's Cons:

[list]
    [*]  - The game is dying for voice actors. 
    [*]  - At times, it feels as though you are being lead.
    [*]  - The game is really designed for a single playthrough.
[/list]


Overall I liked the game, and I think if its on sale its a definite purchase. What it lacks, it makes up for in being a really well thought out game, that kept me interested until the end. At times when I was lost, I felt as though things were given to me, making me feel as though you are being lead, rather than truly discovering things, however it may be that the game needs this to get you there in the end.

I think giving this game a 6 out of 10 is fair, its slightly above average, and being that its really short, I think it could have gotten a higher score if it had a little more. Voice acting would have easily had me giving this a 7 or 8 I think, this game really needed that imo.
